content: Ovarian cancer is the sixth most common cancer affecting women and is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. A frequent complication of advanced or recurrent ovarian cancer is bowel obstruction. Patients experiencing bowel obstruction are typically in poor physical condition and have a limited life expectancy. As a result, the primary goal of managing bowel obstruction in these patients is to maintain their quality of life (QoL) through effective symptom control. The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness and safety of palliative surgery and medical management for bowel obstruction in women with ovarian cancer. Palliative surgery in this context refers to procedures aimed at controlling the cancer, alleviating symptoms, and improving quality of life, rather than attempting to completely remove the cancer. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to February 2009. Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, reference lists of included studies, and expert consultations were also utilized. The inclusion criteria for the review required studies to compare palliative surgery and medical interventions in adult women diagnosed with ovarian cancer who had either complete or partial bowel obstruction. Both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies that employed multivariable statistical adjustments for baseline differences were considered eligible. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Ultimately, only one non-randomized study met the inclusion criteria, and no meta-analyses could be performed due to the limited data. The included study retrospectively analyzed data from 47 women who underwent either palliative surgery (n = 27) or medical management with Octreotide (n = 20). The study reported outcomes such as overall survival, perioperative mortality, and morbidity. Women with poor performance status were excluded from undergoing surgery. Among the women who underwent surgery, six (22%) experienced serious complications, and three (11%) died as a result of these complications. Despite these risks, multivariable analysis revealed that women who underwent surgery had significantly better survival outcomes compared to those who received Octreotide (p < 0.001), after adjusting for key prognostic factors. However, the study did not report the exact magnitude of the survival benefit. Additionally, quality of life (QoL) outcomes were not assessed, and adverse events were not comprehensively documented. The authors concluded that the evidence comparing palliative surgery and medical management for bowel obstruction in ovarian cancer is of low quality. As a result, definitive conclusions regarding the relative benefits and harms of these treatment approaches cannot be made. Furthermore, it is not possible to identify specific subgroups of women who might benefit more from one treatment over the other. However, there is weak evidence suggesting that surgical management may prolong survival in these patients.
